nameStory: The species name 'straminea' comes from the Latin word for straw-colored, referring to this spider's pale, yellowish appearance that blends perfectly with dried grasses and stems. Like other stretch spiders, it gets its common name from its remarkable ability to elongate its body and legs into a stick-like pose when threatened, stretching out along plant stems to become nearly invisible.
description: The Straw-colored Stretch Spider is a slender, pale spider that specializes in building delicate orb webs near water. With its extremely long, thin legs and elongated body, it looks almost like a piece of dried grass or a thin twig when motionless. These spiders typically measure about half an inch in body length, but their leg span can make them appear much larger as they stretch across their webs.

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Extremely elongated, narrow abdomen that feels almost cylindrical, with a thin cephalothorax that gives the whole spider a stick-like appearance

idTips.label: Markings
idTips.description: Pale straw-yellow to light brown coloration throughout, sometimes with faint darker stripes running lengthwise along the abdomen

idTips.label: Web
idTips.description: Delicate orb web with widely-spaced sticky spirals, often built at an angle over water or damp areas, feeling almost gossamer-thin to the touch

idTips.label: Behavior
idTips.description: When disturbed, stretches legs forward and backward along plant stems, becoming remarkably rigid and motionless like a dried twig

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Body length around 12-15mm, but appears much longer due to stretched posture and extremely long, thin legs

habitat: Found along edges of ponds, streams, marshes, and wetlands throughout New England, typically building webs among cattails, sedges, and other waterside vegetation. These spiders prefer areas with consistent moisture where flying insects are abundant, often positioning their webs just above the water surface or among dense stands of emergent plants.

seasonality.spring: Adults begin appearing in late spring, with females starting to build their characteristic webs over water as temperatures warm and insect activity increases.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when adults are most easily spotted in their webs, especially during early morning when dew makes the delicate web structure visible.
seasonality.fall: Mating occurs and egg sacs are produced, with spiders remaining active until first hard frosts. Look for stretched-out individuals on dying vegetation.
seasonality.winter: Adults typically don't survive freezing temperatures, overwintering as eggs or juveniles in protected areas near their aquatic habitats.

funFact: When perfectly aligned along a plant stem in its defensive stretch pose, this spider can become so convincing as a piece of dried vegetation that even experienced naturalists will walk right past it, only noticing it when it suddenly moves to catch prey in its web.
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with other stretch spiders in the same genus, but the consistently pale, straw-colored appearance without prominent dark markings helps distinguish it from the more colorful Green Long-jawed Orbweaver or the larger Common Stretch Spider.
contextualKnowledge: This species is quite rare in New England with only a single confirmed observation, making it a special find for spider enthusiasts. The Tetragnatha genus name means 'four jaws' in Greek, referring to their prominent chelicerae (jaw-like mouthparts) that extend forward like tiny tusks.
compareHints: Compared to its relatives, the Straw-colored Stretch Spider is consistently paler than the bright green T. viridis and lacks the bold markings often seen in T. extensa. It's also typically smaller than T. elongata and has a more uniform coloration than the variable T. versicolor, making its pale, straw-like appearance its most reliable distinguishing feature.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among its Tetragnatha relatives, the Green Long-jawed Orbweaver stands out with its vivid green coloration, while the Common Stretch Spider tends to be more yellowish or brownish, and the Silver Long-jawed Orbweaver has distinctive metallic silver markings.
Among New England's long-jawed orbweavers, the Common Stretch Spider is distinguished by its extreme elongation and distinctive straight-line defensive posture.
Among its stretch spider relatives, the Elongate Stilt Spider has the most extreme body elongation - much more stretched than the Common Stretch Spider or Green Long-jawed Orbweaver.
Unlike the Green Long-jawed Orbweaver that stays near water and has greenish coloring, versicolor prefers dry areas and shows yellow-orange tones.

Among the Tetragnatha genus in New England, the Silver Long-jawed Orbweaver stands out for its distinctive metallic silvery appearance, while the Green Long-jawed Orbweaver appears more yellow-green and the Common Stretch Spider tends to be brownish.
Unlike the Common Stretch Spider which has a more uniform abdomen, the tailed long-jawed orbweaver has that distinctive rear projection.
